variables.name: grid/columns

variables.name: grid/gutter

variables.name: grid/margin/mobile

variables.name: grid/margin/tablet

variables.name: layout/bar/height
variables.description: The government accessibility bar. Genuinely fixed: it carries one row of controls at a known size, in every surface and every locale.

variables.name: layout/chatbot/width
variables.description: Panel width at rest. Wide enough for a 246px bubble to hold a readable measure and still leave the column its gutters; narrow enough not to cover the page it is helping with.

variables.name: layout/chatbot/height
variables.description: Panel height at rest. A ceiling, not a floor: the panel caps against the shared corner rail via `100dvh - rail - launcher - gaps`, so on a short viewport it is shorter than this.

variables.name: layout/chatbot/launcher
variables.description: Launcher diameter, and the closed widget's whole footprint. Well past the 24px WCAG 2.2 (2.5.8) target minimum, because it is the one control on the page a citizen may be hunting for.

variables.name: layout/chatbot/bubbleMax
variables.description: Message bubble cap — 67% of the 368px content column, so the transcript never reads as a wall of text. CSS expresses it as the ratio rather than this number, so the cap follows the column if the panel width ever changes; this token is that ratio resolved at the default width, for Figma to bind.

variables.name: layout/chatbot/typingDot
variables.description: Diameter of one dot in the typing indicator. Four of them, 110ms apart. Was recorded as 6 in the library while both the master and the stylesheet drew 5 — the variable was carried but never bound.

variables.name: layout/flag/width
variables.description: The Indian flag mark in the accessibility bar. Fixed so the bar's left edge is identical across the estate.

variables.name: layout/masthead/minHeight
variables.description: The brand row's MINIMUM, not its height. It hugs its content, which varies: two or three lines of ministry lockup, an optional BETA badge, a search field on the website, an account block on portals. 72 is the floor that keeps the emblem legible when the lockup is shortest. Never lay out against a fixed masthead height — see `layout/chrome/minHeight`.

variables.name: layout/chrome/minHeight
variables.description: Accessibility bar plus brand row at their minimum — the offset the sidebar and content start at on a portal page. Use it for a scroll anchor or a sticky offset, NOT to size the shell: the brand row hugs, so the real value moves with the content. AppShell lays the shell out as a three-row grid (`auto auto 1fr`) so nothing subtracts this from the viewport. At the documented content the navbar measures 134 including its shadow, of which 118 is the layout box.

variables.name: layout/sidebar/width
variables.description: The portal sidebar's expanded width. Genuinely fixed: the nav labels are known copy, and a fluid sidebar would move the content edge on every route. Its inner padding is `padding/m` (16), leaving a 268 item column; items are `target/spacious` (48) tall. Below the tablet breakpoint the sidebar is not narrowed — it becomes a drawer.

variables.name: layout/sidebar/collapsedWidth
variables.description: The portal sidebar's collapsed width: a 56px icon row plus 16px padding each side. Fixed for the same reason as `layout/sidebar/width` — the content edge must not move between routes. Below the tablet breakpoint the rail is a drawer, never this width.

variables.name: layout/sidebar/flyoutWidth
variables.description: Width of the panel a collapsed rail opens beside a Group item to list its level-2 pages. Fixed so the panel does not resize with its longest label.

variables.name: layout/login/hero/width
variables.description: Desktop hero column carrying the portal photograph, brand lockup and the signing-into bar.

variables.name: layout/login/panel/width
variables.description: Desktop auth form panel. 1440 - 922 = 518.

variables.name: layout/login/panel/gutter
variables.description: Horizontal inset of the form panel and the hero content. The space scale jumps 32 -> 120, so this sits between them deliberately.

variables.name: layout/login/content/width
variables.description: The form content column itself. 518 - 2x64 = 390. Every auth field, button and divider is this wide.

variables.name: layout/tab/indicator
variables.description: Thickness of the selected tab's underline or rail. Deliberately NOT `control/border/width`: this is a selection mark that happens to be a line, not a control edge, so it must not move when the form-control hairline is retuned.

variables.name: layout/tab/track
variables.description: Inset between an enclosed track and the pills inside it — the track's own padding, and the indicator's top/bottom inset. Small enough that the track reads as a frame around the pills rather than a panel containing them.

variables.name: target/min
variables.description: The absolute floor — WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA. Use ONLY where the spacing exception is genuinely satisfied or the target is inline in a sentence. Anything a citizen must hit on a phone deserves `comfortable`.

variables.name: target/comfortable
variables.description: WCAG 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), Level AAA, and Apple's Human Interface Guidelines minimum (44pt). The right default for a public government service: it clears the AA floor with room to spare and matches what iOS users' fingers are calibrated to.

variables.name: target/spacious
variables.description: Material Design 3 / Android's minimum touch target (48dp). Use for primary actions and anything used one-handed on the move — this is the largest of the three published floors, so meeting it satisfies all of them.

variables.name: target/spacing
variables.description: Minimum gap BETWEEN adjacent targets — Material 3's 8dp separation. It is also what makes WCAG 2.5.8's spacing exception reachable: separation, not size, is what stops a 24px target being mis-tapped.

variables.name: cmp/badge/dotSize
variables.description: The status/unread DOT — ONE definition for the whole estate, not one per component. Bound by the Badge's dot and by Tabs' badge; when this moves, every dot moves. It is 6 and not the on-grid 8 on purpose: beside 14px label text an 8px dot reads as a bullet rather than a signal, and 6 is what Material and Carbon both publish. A literal rather than an alias because no ref/size step is 6, and inventing one would add a scale step for a single affordance — the same reasoning layout/bar/height (46) and layout/flag/width (33) already follow. Authored in Figma first; reconciled into code 2026-08-18.

variables.name: cmp/badge/dotSizeLg
variables.description: The dot beside 16px body text — Badge size=lg, and Tabs size=L. A dot is sized against the TYPE it annotates, not against its container, which is why this steps with the type scale and not with the control height.

variables.name: cmp/accessibilityBar/height
variables.description: Bar height. ALIASES 46px rather than repeating 46px — until 2026-08-18 both carried the literal independently, so moving one silently left the other behind. layout/bar/height is the published Figma name the master binds to; this is the component-scoped handle the CSS uses.

variables.name: cmp/accessibilityBar/flagWidth
variables.description: Flag/emblem chip width. ALIASES 33px rather than repeating 33px — same duplicate-literal defect as `height`, fixed 2026-08-18. Height is 1.375rem, making a 3:2 chip.

variables.name: cmp/accessibilityBar/flagHeight

variables.name: cmp/accessibilityBar/pillSize

variables.name: cmp/accessibilityBar/stepSize

variables.name: cmp/accessibilityBar/launchIconSize

variables.name: cmp/accessibilityBar/iconButtonSize

variables.name: cmp/divider/width

variables.name: border/neutral/subtle
variables.description: Use for a hairline that separates without drawing the eye — dividers and card edges. Contrast 1.35:1 vs bg/neutral/base — no guaranteed contrast class; treat as a boundary, not as text.

variables.name: border/neutral/base
variables.description: Use for a standard boundary. Contrast 1.66:1 vs bg/neutral/base — no guaranteed contrast class; treat as a boundary, not as text.

variables.name: border/neutral/bolder/default
variables.description: Form control border, resting. Rung 500 since 2026-09-04: rung 400 (#8e949c) was 3.06:1 on white — a hairline pass of 1.4.11 — and 2.68:1 on bg/neutral/subtler, the ground most forms actually sit on, which is a FAIL. 500 measures 4.65:1 on white and 4.07:1 on the muted ground. Hover steps to 600. Contrast 4.65:1 vs bg/neutral/base — meets ≥4.5:1: text-safe (WCAG 1.4.3 AA).

variables.name: border/neutral/inverse/default
variables.description: Border/rule ink on a dark or brand surface — the inverse of border/neutral/base. Nested as inverse/default rather than a bare `inverse` leaf because it has a `subtle` sibling, which is the same shape border/neutral/bolder already uses (bolder/default, bolder/hover). Aliases `color/neutralScale/0`, as `subtle` does, so the pair moves together if the neutral ramp's white is ever retuned.

variables.name: border/neutral/inverse/subtle
variables.description: The quieter inverse rule — white (neutralScale/0) at alpha/40, authored as a reference plus an opacity reference since 2026-09-04 rather than a pre-composited rgba(). Used by Divider Tone=Inverse subtle and the AccessibilityBar's separators. The Figma variable was `border/neutral/inverse-subtle` until 2026-08-18 — a hyphen inside a segment, which grammar RULE 1 forbids; renamed IN PLACE so bindings followed. Contrast 3.81:1 vs bg/neutral/inverse — no guaranteed contrast class; treat as a boundary, not as text.

variables.name: border/neutral/selected
variables.description: The edge of a selected control — a checked selection card, a chosen chip, a current tab's rail. Brand 500, the same rung as focus/ring, so ‘selected’ and ‘focused’ share a colour and differ by geometry (a ring stands off the control; this edge is the control's own).

variables.name: bg/neutral/base
variables.description: Use for the ordinary, quietest fill — page and card surfaces that must not compete with their content.

variables.name: bg/neutral/subtler
variables.description: Use for a barely-there tint, for hovered rows and zebra striping. Contrast 1.14:1 vs bg/neutral/base — no guaranteed contrast class; treat as a fill, not as text.

variables.name: bg/neutral/hover
variables.description: The neutral hover wash — a row, a menu item, a plain icon button responding to the pointer. Same rung as bg/neutral/subtler by design: hover on a neutral surface is one step of tint, not a new colour. Bind this, not subtler, so a hover can be retuned without moving every quiet surface.

variables.name: bg/neutral/active
variables.description: The neutral pressed wash — one step past hover, held while the pointer is down or the row is being acted on. Pairs with bg/neutral/hover the way overlay/brand/active pairs with overlay/brand/hover.

variables.name: bg/neutral/selected
variables.description: The selected row, item or navigation entry — the brand's lightest tint, so selection reads as ‘chosen’ rather than ‘hovered’ even on a neutral list. The sidebar's current page and a data table's chosen row bind it. Selected is a STATE the reader set; hover is one the pointer set.

variables.name: bg/neutral/readonly
variables.description: A read-only field's ground: quieter than an editable field, and NOT the disabled fill — the value is the point and stays readable and selectable. forms.css binds it on [readonly] inputs.

variables.name: bg/neutral/loading
variables.description: The resting fill of a loading skeleton, under the shimmer — a surface in its LOADING state. Its own role so a skeleton can be retuned without touching the surfaces it stands in for; motion/loading/pulse carries the shimmer's timing.

variables.name: text/neutral/bolder
variables.description: Use for max-contrast headings that need to outrank surrounding text. Contrast 16.59:1 vs bg/neutral/base and bg/neutral/subtler — meets ≥4.5:1: max-contrast headings (WCAG 1.4.3 AA).

variables.name: text/link/brand/default
variables.description: Text-link colour. Decoupled from action.primary so it can be lighter on dark surfaces (≥4.5:1 as text) without weakening white-on-primary button contrast. BLUE IS RAMP 600, NOT 500, and the reason is the ground it actually sits on: 500 (#0373df) measures 4.64:1 on white but 4.07:1 on bg/surface/muted, which is the class the estate's own <body> carries — so the link failed 1.4.3 on most pages while passing every check. 600 (#005eb9) is 6.36:1 and 5.57:1. It passed because the contrast contract judges text against bg/neutral/base, i.e. white; that surface assumption is recorded as an open item rather than widened here, since widening it re-judges every text token at once. Navy holds ramp 500 through its own colorModes override and already clears 4.5:1 on that ground. dbim has no such override, so it follows the base step and moved to 600 with it across all six of its hues — which only darkens those links, never lightens them. Contrast 5.57:1 vs bg/neutral/base and bg/neutral/subtler — meets ≥4.5:1: text (WCAG 1.4.3 AA).

variables.name: focus/ring
variables.description: The keyboard focus ring. SOLID since 2026-09-04: it was rgba(3,115,223,.48), which flattens on white to #86bcf0 — 2.01:1 against the 3:1 that WCAG 2.2 1.4.11 asks of a focus indicator — and 53 outline rules across chips, search, controls and the auth stack still read it after forms.css alone was corrected on 2026-09-03. It now aliases the brand key colour, which is 4.64:1 on white and 4.07:1 on the muted page in Blue, and follows Navy and the DBIM modes through the alias. Paint it as `outline: var(--sa-focus-width) solid var(--sa-focus-ring)` with `outline-offset: var(--sa-focus-offset)`, never as a box-shadow — a shadow is not painted in Windows High Contrast Mode.

variables.name: focus/ringInner
variables.description: The inner ring of a two-tone focus indicator — white, laid between the control and focus/ring so the ring stays visible on a brand or dark surface where blue-on-blue would vanish (WCAG 2.4.13 asks for 3:1 against adjacent colours). In CSS: box-shadow 0 0 0 focus/offset focus/ringInner, then the outline; in Figma the focus/ring effect style binds its inner spread to it.

variables.name: overlay/neutral/boldest
variables.description: The scrim behind a modal — the brand's neutral 800 at alpha/48, as a REFERENCE plus an OPACITY reference. Until 2026-09-04 this was an rgba() literal with six hand-authored DBIM copies, because a literal in the single-mode Color collection is frozen at whatever brand was current when it was typed — and Navy once inherited the Blue neutral (#1E2124 for #1E2024) without anyone seeing it. Figma can now alias a colour and keep a separate opacity, so the copies are gone: the scrim follows neutralScale/800 through Blue, Navy and every DBIM mode by construction.

variables.name: overlay/neutral/hover
variables.description: State layer for hover on a NEUTRAL surface — ink at 4%, laid over whatever the surface is. Material 3's hover layer; the brand counterpart is overlay/brand/hover. Use where a surface must keep its own colour under the interaction (an image tile, a coloured card) and bg/neutral/hover would replace it.

variables.name: overlay/neutral/active
variables.description: State layer for pressed on a neutral surface — ink at 8%. One step past hover, like every pressed state in the system.

variables.name: overlay/neutral/focus
variables.description: State layer for a focused surface that has no ring of its own — a focused list row, a focused card — ink at 16%. The ring (focus/ring) remains the primary focus indicator; this is the tint beneath it, never a replacement.

variables.name: overlay/neutral/drag
variables.description: State layer for a surface being dragged — ink at 8%, with elevation/raised. A dragged row is lifted and tinted so it reads as detached from the list beneath it.

variables.name: overlay/brand/hover
variables.description: Hover wash on a brand-coloured surface. 8%, matching the published Figma variable and the AccessibilityBar's States documentation. This family was authored here at 12% from a base that predated 33cbb4f, which had already corrected the component from 12% to 8%; reconciled to 8% on 2026-08-19.

variables.description: Pressed/selected wash on a brand-coloured surface. Named `active`, not `pressed` — `active` is the state word the whole system uses (cmp/action/*/active/bg), and the grammar has no `pressed`.

variables.name: ref/font/family/display
variables.description: The optical Display cut, for the 40-80px Display ramp. Noto Sans ships two cuts of one design: the text cut is drawn for reading at 12-24px, and at 80px its open spacing reads as loose. The Display cut tightens it. This is now genuinely LOADED (apps/hub root layout, weight 500) — for a long time it was named here and loaded nowhere, so it fell through to the text cut and the matching Figma variable could not resolve at all. LATIN ONLY: `Noto Sans Display` has no Devanagari subset and `Noto Sans Devanagari` has no Display cut, so a Hindi heading falls through to Noto Sans by design. In Figma the same cut is a STYLE of Noto Sans ("Display Medium"), not a family — see design.md. Raw type step. Prefer a text style from the Display / Headline / Title / Body / Label ramp — these are the parts those styles are assembled from.

variables.name: ref/font/family/mono
variables.description: CODE AND TECHNICAL STRINGS ONLY — token names, CSS snippets, file paths in the design-system docs. NOT for numbers, amounts or reference numbers: those want `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` on Noto Sans, which aligns digits down a column while keeping them in the same typeface as the text beside them. Switching a data column to a monospace face is the clumsier fix and looks like a different design. The estate already does this correctly in the Aadhaar/PAN field, the charts, the SLA indicator and the shared DataTable. DELIBERATELY a system stack: `ui-monospace` resolves to the platform's own mono (SF Mono, Cascadia, Roboto Mono) — all well-drawn, all disambiguating 0/O and 1/l/I, and already on the device. A webfont here would download on every page to style sample code on a handful of documentation pages, which on a low-bandwidth government audience is not a trade worth making. IBM Plex Mono was set here briefly and reverted for that reason. Raw type step. Prefer a text style from the Display / Headline / Title / Body / Label ramp — these are the parts those styles are assembled from.

variables.name: ref/font/family/icon
variables.description: The ICON face — Material Symbols Rounded, the official SAMAVESH icon system. It is here for the same reason every other family is: a Material Symbols glyph is TEXT, not artwork, so its family is a typographic decision the design system owns rather than a constant three files happen to agree on. Before this token the name was a literal in `icons.css` (twice) and in all seven Figma `Icon/*` text styles, which is four places to change and no way to prove they still match. variables.name: ref/breakpoint/laptop
variables.description: The third anchor, and the one the ladder was missing. Between tablet (768) and desktop (1280) sat a 512px void with no token in it — which is where iPad landscape, 11-13" laptops and every half-screen window on a 2K monitor live. Anything needing to change at 1024 had to hardcode it or round to one of the neighbours. Matches Tailwind's `lg`, so the token and the utility variant used across this estate finally agree. Viewport anchor. The ladder follows Material 3's window size classes, which are derived from measured device distribution rather than from one framework's grid: compact <600, medium 600-839, expanded 840-1199, large 1200-1599, extra-large >=1600. UX4G publishes the two content widths but no breakpoints at all, so there is nothing to diverge FROM here; where its guidance and interface quality met, quality won, per .claude/rules/standards-precedence.md. Recorded in docs/guidelines/README.md. Viewport anchor: the laptop width at which the layout changes. A media query cannot read a variable, so nothing binds this — the Viewport collection's modes carry what it SELECTS (container/page, grid/margin/page). Documented on /design-system/foundations/breakpoints.

variables.description: Where the sidebar and content sit side by side and the page cap of 1200 engages. Viewport anchor: the desktop width at which the layout changes. A media query cannot read a variable, so nothing binds this — the Viewport collection's modes carry what it SELECTS (container/page, grid/margin/page). Documented on /design-system/foundations/breakpoints.

variables.name: ref/breakpoint/desktopXl
variables.description: Where the content cap widens from `container/content` (1200) to `container/contentXl` (1320). 1768 -> 1600 -> 1440 over 2026-08-24, each step decided by measuring the page rather than by citing a ladder. 1768 was abandoned because a 1728-wide viewport carried 264px of margin each side against 1768's own 224px — margins NARROWING as the screen grew. 1600 (Material 3's extra-large window class) was then abandoned because it left the ladder's WEAKEST POINT sitting on its most common viewport: at 1536 — 1920 at 125% Windows scaling, the single most common desktop width — content held only 75% of the screen, worse than at 1280 (90%) and worse than at 1600 (78%). 1440 fixes the range that carries the most users: 1440 goes 80% -> 88%, 1512 76% -> 84%, 1536 75% -> 83%. Nothing at 1600 and above changes. THE FLOOR THAT WAS DROPPED, deliberately: earlier notes held that 1440 must stay on the 1200 cap because UX4G says '1200px desktop'. UX4G publishes no breakpoints at all, so it never fixed where desktop ends; and `.claude/rules/standards-precedence.md` puts interface quality above it, which is the whole point of that rule. Recorded as divergence #6 in docs/guidelines/README.md. It also makes the code agree with the Handoff, whose Home frame draws a 1320 container on a 1440 artboard — the frame was right and the note calling it wrong has been withdrawn. Not part of the type curve — `clamp()` still tops out at 1280, so this anchor resizes no glyph. Viewport anchor: the desktopXl width at which the layout changes. A media query cannot read a variable, so nothing binds this — the Viewport collection's modes carry what it SELECTS (container/page, grid/margin/page). Documented on /design-system/foundations/breakpoints.

variables.name: ref/breakpoint/desktopWide
variables.description: The fifth anchor, where the cap widens a second time to `container/contentWide` (1440). Without it a 2560-wide monitor rendered a 1320 column between 620px margins — 48% of the screen given to nothing, which is the complaint that started this. One step is not enough for the range 1600-2560+: a single cap either starves the desktop or sprawls on the monitor. Stops at 1440 rather than continuing to grow because beyond that a 12-column grid starts costing more in eye travel than it returns in density. Viewport anchor. The ladder follows Material 3's window size classes, which are derived from measured device distribution rather than from one framework's grid: compact <600, medium 600-839, expanded 840-1199, large 1200-1599, extra-large >=1600. UX4G publishes the two content widths but no breakpoints at all, so there is nothing to diverge FROM here; where its guidance and interface quality met, quality won, per .claude/rules/standards-precedence.md. Recorded in docs/guidelines/README.md. Viewport anchor: the desktopWide width at which the layout changes. A media query cannot read a variable, so nothing binds this — the Viewport collection's modes carry what it SELECTS (container/page, grid/margin/page). Documented on /design-system/foundations/breakpoints.

variables.description: 540px — UX4G 3.0's Bootstrap container step, carried for parity with the standard. The estate's own content column is `container/page`; use this rung only where a UX4G component is transcribed as published.

variables.name: container/2xl
variables.description: Completes UX4G's container ladder, which is Bootstrap's: 540 / 720 / 960 / 1140 / 1320. It was the one step missing here, so `contentXl` had to restate the literal; it now aliases this.

variables.name: container/content
variables.description: The desktop content cap. Changed from 1280px to UX4G 3.0's published 1200px on 13 August 2026 ('Grid and layout': max content width 1200px desktop, 1320px desktop XL). Until then the estate ran FOUR widths at once — this token said 1280 and nothing consumed it, 22 website section files hardcoded the same 1280 as a literal, SiteHeader defaulted to 1320, and PortalLoginShell's chrome used 1536. The visible defect was that above 1320px the masthead's content ran 20px wider each side than the page beneath it, so the National Emblem did not line up with the content column. At the 1440 design frame 1200 leaves a 120px margin either side, comfortably clear of the 32px `grid/margin/desktop` floor. BIND `container/page` INSTEAD unless you specifically mean this rung: `page` carries a mode per viewport and resolves to the right rung on its own. This one is fixed at every window size.

variables.name: container/contentXl
variables.description: The content cap above `breakpoint/desktopXl`. Aliases `container/2xl` rather than restating 1320, so the estate's cap and UX4G's ladder cannot drift apart. UX4G publishes the value but not the point at which it engages, so the anchor is the estate's own `breakpoint/desktopXl` — 1440 since 2026-08-24 (it read 1768, then 1600, before the page itself was measured). Bootstrap's `container-xxl` at 1400 was considered and rejected: at 1400 the 1440 design frame would take this cap, contradicting the 1200-at-desktop guidance. (This note said 1400 WAS the anchor until 2026-08-24; it never was — the token has read 1768, then 1600, and now 1440.) BIND `container/page` INSTEAD unless you specifically mean this rung: `page` carries a mode per viewport and resolves to the right rung on its own. This one is fixed at every window size.

variables.name: container/contentWide
variables.description: The content cap at `breakpoint/desktopWide` (1920) and above — the third and last step of the page container (1200 -> 1320 -> 1440). Exists because two steps left a 2560-wide monitor rendering a 1320 column between 620px margins. Stops here rather than tracking the viewport: past ~1440 a 12-column grid costs more in eye travel than it returns in density, and the line lengths inside it stop being scannable. Consumed only through `--sa-container-page` in foundations/layout.css; never restate it in a component. BIND `container/page` INSTEAD unless you specifically mean this rung: `page` carries a mode per viewport and resolves to the right rung on its own. This one is fixed at every window size.

variables.name: container/wide

variables.name: container/page
variables.description: The RESOLVED page cap at a given window size — what `.sa-container` actually applies, and the one container token a page skeleton should bind. `content`/`contentXl`/`contentWide` are the three rungs; this is which rung is in force. It carries a mode per viewport, so a designer opening a frame in Desktop XL sees 1320 without having to know the media query that picks it. That was previously impossible: the CSS derived `--sa-container-page` in a media query, and a Figma variable cannot express a media query, so the cap was the one layout value the library could not represent at all. $value is the mobile-first base, which is `content` — the cap is 1200 everywhere below 1600.

variables.name: grid/margin/page
variables.description: The RESOLVED page margin at a given window size — the companion to `container/page`, and what `.sa-container` applies as its inline padding. `mobile`/`tablet`/`desktop` are the three rungs; this is which rung is in force. It steps with the CAP, not with the viewport anchors: a wider margin only buys breathing room while the container is still fluid, and once the cap binds it buys nothing and costs content. Stepping it at the desktop anchor did exactly that — content went 1152 -> 1136 crossing 1280 — so Laptop, Desktop and Desktop XL hold the tablet rung and the 32px step waits for Desktop Wide. Keeping 24 at Desktop XL is also what makes the content there exactly 1272 — the width the Handoff's own frame draws. $value is the mobile-first base.

contrast.$description: Contrast classes are MEASURED against each token's own surface, across every brand, and the worst case is what the description states. A token absent from this summary carries no contrast sentence because the prominence ladder does not describe it — see build/contrast-contract.mjs.
